title: Influenza A Cases Rise Across India as Covid-19 Returns During Monsoon
excerpt: Hospitals in Mumbai, Andhra Pradesh, and other states report a simultaneous climb in influenza A and fresh Covid-19 infections as the monsoon season triggers its annual wave of respiratory illness.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Influenza A cases are rising in India, coinciding with a fresh wave of Covid-19.
  • Mumbai hospitals report over seven daily positive cases of Covid-19 or H1N1.
  • Andhra Pradesh logged 12 Covid-19 cases and four deaths since late June.
  • Doctors recommend hygiene and masks, especially for vulnerable populations.
  • Influenza activity is low but trending upward as monsoon season approaches.
  • WHO FluNet data for the week of July 6–12 shows influenza activity in India is low but on a rising trend, with monsoon-season peaks historically running from July through October.
  • Mumbai hospitals are detecting more than seven positive cases of Covid-19 or H1N1 daily, alongside influenza A and RSV, with some patients requiring hospitalisation for severe lung infections.
  • Andhra Pradesh has reported 12 Covid-19 cases and four deaths since June 26; nationwide, 339 cases were logged from July 1, with Kerala (115), Karnataka (64), and Maharashtra (43) leading.
  • Doctors advise hand hygiene, masks in crowded settings, and prompt medical attention for high fever or breathing difficulty — especially for older adults, pregnant women, and those with chronic conditions.

Multiple Viruses Circulating Simultaneously

India's monsoon season is driving a familiar but unwelcome pattern: a simultaneous rise in influenza A subtypes H1N1 and H3N2, fresh Covid-19 infections, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) across major cities.

In Mumbai, laboratories at Breach Candy Hospital are flagging more than seven positive cases of either Covid-19 or H1N1 every day, according to a report by the Times of India. Bombay Hospital physician Dr Gautam Bhansali described the situation bluntly.

"Viruses are ruling right now. We are seeing swine flu, influenza A and RSV. They cause high-grade fever and severe lung infection, needing hospitalisation."

— Dr Gautam Bhansali, Physician, Bombay Hospital

"Historically, India's influenza wave does not peak until August or September, meaning the current numbers likely represent the early stages of a seasonal climb.</p>"

"Historically, India's influenza wave does not peak until August or September, meaning the current numbers likely represent the early stages of a seasonal climb.</p>"

Senior physician Dr Hemant Thacker said his outpatient department is seeing fresh Covid cases daily. "We saw a lot of swine flu over the last month, but in the last 7–10 days, Covid has also begun showing up," he told the Times of India.

Covid-19 Cases Resurface Across States

The fresh Covid-19 wave, though modest, has triggered heightened vigilance. Andhra Pradesh reported 12 confirmed cases and four deaths between June 26 and July 16, according to the state health department. The deceased patients all had severe underlying conditions including hypertension and diabetes. Five samples have been sent to the National Institute of Virology in Pune for genome sequencing to identify the circulating variant.

Nationwide, 339 Covid-19 cases were registered from July 1 through mid-July, with Kerala recording 115, Karnataka 64, Maharashtra 43, Tamil Nadu 39, and Delhi 18, according to The Hindu Business Line. Karnataka has stepped up surveillance in districts bordering Andhra Pradesh, with officials in Tumakuru implementing precautionary measures in border taluks.

The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare said it is closely monitoring the situation but stressed there is no cause for alarm.

Influenza Trend Rising Ahead of Monsoon Peak

WHO FluNet sentinel surveillance data for the week of July 6–12 (Week 28) classifies influenza activity in India as "low" but notes the trend is rising. India's influenza pattern is bimodal: one peak runs through the monsoon months of July to October, and a second builds during the cooler January to March window, according to InfectRisk, which aggregates WHO data.

A multi-centre surveillance study covering 45,320 patients across 12 sentinel sites in western India between 2020 and 2024, published in the Journal of Clinical and Community Practice, found that H1N1 was the predominant strain at 49.5 percent of influenza-positive cases, followed by H3N2 at 25.4 percent. Monsoon months accounted for 54.2 percent of all confirmed cases. H3N2 carried higher hospitalisation rates (32 percent) and mortality (2.1 percent) compared with other subtypes.

Doctors Urge Precautions, Not Panic

Dr Suranjit Chatterjee, Senior Consultant in Internal Medicine at Indraprastha Apollo Hospital in Delhi, said the monsoon season typically sees a rise in viral infections and urged routine precautions rather than alarm.

"Older adults, pregnant women, and people with chronic illnesses should remain especially careful during this period. Maintaining good hand hygiene, ensuring proper ventilation, and staying home if you develop symptoms can help reduce the spread."

— Dr Suranjit Chatterjee, Indraprastha Apollo Hospital, Delhi

Dr Mohsin Wali of Sir Ganga Ram Hospital echoed the message: "We have to learn to live with Covid. There is no need to worry. However, people with comorbidities should be extra cautious." He added that Covid-appropriate behaviour should be followed at large public gatherings.

Doctors recommend early medical consultation if fever persists beyond three days or is accompanied by breathing difficulty. Antiviral drugs such as oseltamivir are most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset. The annual influenza vaccine, available in India, remains underused — coverage stands at roughly 12 percent nationally, according to the western India surveillance study.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad planning monsoon-season travel to India, the dual flu-and-Covid uptick is a practical planning factor. Travellers visiting elderly relatives — particularly in affected states like Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, and Maharashtra — should consider getting an annual flu shot before departure and carrying masks for crowded indoor settings. Those with chronic conditions or compromised immunity should consult their physician about antiviral prophylaxis.

What Comes Next

Genome sequencing results from samples sent to Pune's NIV will clarify which Covid variant is circulating. If a new subvariant is identified, it could influence whether authorities recommend updated boosters. The WHO's next FluNet update, due around July 23, will reveal whether the rising trend has accelerated as the monsoon deepens. Historically, India's influenza wave does not peak until August or September, meaning the current numbers likely represent the early stages of a seasonal climb.
